idiom_name: Azure Service Bus ServiceBusProcessor (ProcessMessageAsync handler); MSMQ ReceiveCompleted as the classic shape
implementation_notes: The .NET realisation is an event-based processor: ServiceBusProcessor exposes ProcessMessageAsync and ProcessErrorAsync handlers plus StartProcessingAsync/StopProcessingAsync for lifecycle; the handler receives a ServiceBusReceivedMessage that carries its own Complete/Abandon/DeadLetter operations, and MaxConcurrentCalls, PrefetchCount and ReceiveMode are the delivery policy. What replaces the classic consumer is that the SDK owns the receive loop and lock renewal, settling the message after the handler returns when AutoCompleteMessages is set. The legacy shape is System.Messaging.MessageQueue's ReceiveCompleted event, raised by BeginReceive() - it is .NET Framework-only (System.Messaging.dll), so new code should stay with a modern processor; the same event model exists in RabbitMQ.Client's EventingBasicConsumer for AMQP.
pitfalls: ProcessErrorAsync is mandatory: a delivery or transport error without an error handler faults the processor.
With AutoCompleteMessages=true the message is settled as soon as the handler returns; an exception makes it redeliver, so handlers must be idempotent.
MaxConcurrentCalls and PrefetchCount together decide in-flight work; a large prefetch with slow handlers lets message locks expire and messages be delivered twice.
StopProcessingAsync awaits in-flight handlers, then Close/DisposeAsync releases the receiver links and sessions - abandoning the processor leaks them.
